newsitem.title: USA: Westin "Who are you sleeping with" ad sparks reaction.
newsitem.headline: Westin "Who are you sleeping with" ad sparks reaction.

text.p: Apparently, some women don't find Westin Hotels & Resorts' advertising campaign a bit funny.

At issue is a TV spot featuring a woman executive at a Westin hotel, while a voice in the background asks, "Who is she sleeping with?" The ad concludes with the answer, "Westin. Choose your travel partner wisely."

Chicago Tribune columnist Carol Kleiman Tuesday in her syndicated Women at Work column took issue with the ad, reacting to a number of e-mail messages and calls from women who believe the ad reinforces the stereotype of women sleeping their way up the corporate ladder.
Kleiman said she has received 25 complaints about Westin's advertising, and expects to hear more.
While it's "not horribly offensive," Westin's ad doesn't do women any good either, said Jane Tobler, spokeswoman for Business and Professional Women/USA, a non-profit group representing 70,000 women.
"With women CEOs making up less than 7 percent of Fortune 500 companies, women haven't reached equity in the workplace," said Tobler.

"Media and advertising shouldn't further impede women's rise to the top by perpetuating negative stereotypes. With the 'Who is she sleeping with line,' the connotation is that she didn't make it to the top because of her skills, education and expertise, but because of her sensuality," Tobler said.
Seattle-based Westin Hotels & Resorts knew it was taking a chance with its campaign, created by DDB Needham Chicago.
"Whenever you run provocative ads, there is a risk involved," said Sue Brush, vice president-advertising and public relations for Westin.

When Westin launched the $25 million global campaign in May, it was looking to grab the attention of business travelers. "They didn't want two mints on a pillow advertising," said DDB Needham spokeswoman Dorothy Denzler. "They wanted something to break through the clutter."
The ads, created by an all-woman creative team, were meant to be inclusive, said Carolyn Bergen, copywriter and associate creative director.

"Had we not done a spot about women, we felt that would have been sexist." Bergen said the creative team in no way meant for the advertising to be offensive. "We feel that women have achieved enough that they can appreciate the irony of the campaign," she said.
Although controversial, the campaign seems to be producing the desired effect for Westin, which reports a 22 percent increase in reservations since the ads broke.

"We know its' good strong advertising," said Brush. "It's received some awards and I'm sure it will continue to do so." The TV campaign will run globally through 1997, with new print executions breaking in February, Brush said.
